expectations.text: The response explains that the loop is latency-bound on the single accumulator `s`: each vfmadd231sd has to wait for the previous one (about 4 cycles), and it cites the annotate evidence (the FMA into %xmm0 carrying ~90% of the samples).
expectations.evidence: [blind LLM grader] response.md:1 '`s += r*r` makes every iteration depend on the one before ... one element per FMA latency, which is 4 cycles on Sapphire Rapids'; :12 quotes the annotate line 'vfmadd231sd %xmm1,%xmm1,%xmm0 # s = r*r + s needs the previous s <- 90% of samples'; :15 'xmm0 holds s ... each FMA has to wait 4 cycles for the previous one'; :18 gives 3.9 cycles/element.

expectations.text: The response notes that the hot loop is scalar double precision (`sd` instructions on xmm registers) even though the CPU supports AVX2/AVX-512, i.e. the loop isn't vectorized.
expectations.evidence: [blind LLM grader] The reply never says the hot loop is scalar. It shows the vmovsd/vsubsd/vfmadd231sd lines (:10-12) without saying that `sd` means scalar double, and the diagnosis never contrasts the loop with the CPU's AVX2/AVX-512 width. The only hint is in the compiler-limit paragraph (:28): the compiler is 'not allowed to split s into partial sums or vectorize the reduction'. AVX-512 comes up only at :86, as a design choice for the fix.

expectations.text: The response explains that the compiler won't reassociate or vectorize this floating-point reduction at -O2 unless allowed to (e.g. -ffast-math/-fassociative-math, `#pragma omp simd reduction`, or a manual rewrite).

Without -ffast-math (or -fassociative-math), neither GCC nor Clang is allowed to split s into partial sums or vectorize the reduction. expectations.evidence: [blind LLM grader] response.md:88-95 'To confirm on the box': 'perf stat -e cycles,instructions ./fitbench --points 100000 --iters 200000' and 'In perf annotate, the samples should now spread across the loads and vsubpd instead of piling onto one FMA'. :53-57 gives the expected 7-12x and 'Judge the result by time or cycles per element, not IPC'.

eval_feedback.overall: 06 accepts 'compare IPC', but after vectorizing, the instruction count falls about as much as the cycle count, so IPC can stay around 1-3 while sse() gets about 10x faster. An answer that told the user to expect IPC 4+ and judge the fix by it would pass 06 while being misleading. Both A (:75) and B (:57) correctly say to judge by cycles or time instead. Consider an assertion for this point. No assertion covers data handling: B sent the user's sse() source to the public godbolt.org API without asking. It disclosed this only after the fact (response.md:110). A kept everything local. No assertion covers untested default code paths: A's AVX-512 intrinsics path becomes the default on the Xeon, but it never ran on AVX-512 hardware. It was only compiled and emulated in C, which A discloses at :119 and asks the user to run sse_check first. B shipped only code it actually ran (AVX2 and SSE2 under Rosetta, arm64), using 256-bit vectors on purpose.
